prayer.text: Saint Francis of Assisi, pray for us.

cues.text: A Merchant's Son Chasing Glory

Born in 1181 or 1182 in Assisi to the wealthy cloth merchant Pietro Bernardone, Francis was baptized Giovanni but called Francesco by his father, out of fondness for France where his business regularly took him.
He spent his youth pursuing the ordinary ambitions of a prosperous young man of his class: fine clothes, popularity among Assisi's young elite, and dreams of chivalric glory.
Those dreams led him, at around twenty, into a local war with the neighboring city of Perugia, where he was captured and held prisoner for roughly a year.
A Voice from the Cross at San Damiano

Released from captivity and slowly recovering from a serious illness that followed, Francis underwent a gradual but decisive conversion, marked by a growing dissatisfaction with his former ambitions and an increasing draw toward prayer and solitude.
Francis was praying before a crucifix in the dilapidated chapel of San Damiano outside Assisi.
By his own account and that of his earliest companions, he heard the crucified Christ speak to him directly: "Francis, go and repair my house, which, as you see, is falling into ruin."
Understanding the command at first quite literally, Francis set about physically rebuilding the small, crumbling chapel with his own hands.
Selling some of his father's cloth to fund the repairs provoked his father's fury and precipitated the dramatic public rupture between them.
Stripped Bare in the Public Square
Brought before the Bishop of Assisi by his outraged father, who demanded either Francis's obedience or the return of every possession his father's money had ever provided him.
Francis responded with a gesture as complete as it was public: he removed every stitch of clothing he was wearing.
Including the very garments his father had paid for, and returned them, declaring that he now recognized only God as his Father.
This total, deliberately public renunciation marked Francis's definitive break with his former life.
From that day forward, he embraced a life of radical poverty, embracing lepers and the poor with a tenderness that had once been foreign to his fastidious younger self.
A Movement No One Planned
Francis's evident joy and total commitment to Gospel poverty drew disciples almost immediately.
By 1210, he had gathered enough companions to seek papal approval for a simple rule of life.
Pope Innocent III granted that approval informally—the founding moment of what would become the Order of Friars Minor .

Within Francis's own lifetime, it grew from a handful of companions to thousands of friars spread across Europe and beyond, genuinely surprising and sometimes troubling Francis, who had never envisioned founding a large, formally organized institution.
The Wounds of Christ Made Visible
In September 1224, two years before his death, Francis retreated to the remote mountain of La Verna to fast and pray in preparation for the feast of St. Michael.
There, according to the earliest and most consistent testimony of his companions, he received a vision of a seraph bearing the likeness of the crucified Christ.
In its wake, he found the stigmata upon his own body — wounds corresponding to those of Christ's hands, feet, and side — and became the first person in recorded Christian history to bear these marks.
With characteristic humility, he attempted to conceal them from all but his closest companions for the remainder of his life.
Legacy
Francis died at the Portiuncula near Assisi on October 3, 1226, and was canonized less than two years later by Pope Gregory IX.
This was one of the most rapid canonizations in Church history, reflecting how immediately and universally his sanctity was recognized even in his own lifetime.
Author of the beloved Canticle of the Sun , praising God through the whole of creation as brothers and sisters, Francis remains among the most universally beloved saints the Church has ever produced.
A wealthy young man's total renunciation of everything the world offered him became, in the end, a joy so luminous and so complete.
That joy continues, eight centuries later, to draw believers and unbelievers alike toward the simple, radical Gospel life he gave up everything to embrace.
